pattern.pick: any 5 questions, at least 2 from each section
pattern.summary: 8 questions in two sections of four. Answer any 5, at least 2 from each section; each carries 10 marks (about 300 words). Some questions are two short notes of 5 marks.
pattern.note: Section I covers stress, its models, proneness and effects; Section II covers coping and management techniques.

choosing: Pick at least 2 from each section — plan 3 from the section you know better.
Models of stress (fight-or-flight, GAS, cognitive appraisal), stress proneness, effects of stress and coping styles come up in almost every paper.
Name the psychologist behind each idea (Selye, Lazarus, Ellis, Seligman) — it strengthens a short answer.

topics.name: Stress Proneness & Moderators
topics.summary: Factors that make a person prone to stress — Type A personality, perfectionism, hostility, learned helplessness and pessimism — and moderators of stress.
points: Stress proneness: a tendency to experience stress more often or more intensely because of personality and thinking patterns.

Type A personality (Friedman and Rosenman): time urgency, impatience, competitiveness, hostility, doing many things at once; the hostility part is linked to heart disease. Type B is relaxed and less stress-prone.
Perfectionism: unrealistically high standards, fear of mistakes, harsh self-criticism — every small failure becomes a stressor.
Hostility: cynical mistrust and anger towards others; keeps the body in a state of arousal.

Learned helplessness (Seligman): after repeated events one cannot control, a person stops trying even when control is possible. Learned pessimism: explaining bad events as permanent, pervasive and personal.
Other factors: low self-esteem, external locus of control, negative thinking, poor coping skills.

Moderators — factors that reduce (or increase) the effect of stress: social support, hardiness (Kobasa: commitment, control, challenge), internal locus of control, self-efficacy, optimism, good coping resources, health and lifestyle.
topics.frame: Meaning → each factor with a one-line example → conclusion on managing it.

topics.name: Stress: Concept, Types, Sources & Measurement
topics.summary: Meaning and nature of stress, types (eustress and distress, acute and chronic), sources, symptoms, and ways to measure stress.
points: Stress (Hans Selye): the body's non-specific response to any demand made on it. A stressor is the demand; stress is the response.
Nature: individual (depends on how a person sees the demand), can be positive or negative, involves body, mind and behaviour.
Types: eustress (positive, motivating) and distress (harmful); acute, episodic acute and chronic stress; hypostress (too little challenge) and hyperstress (overload).

Sources: environmental (noise, pollution, crowding), social (relationships, life events), work or academic (workload, deadlines, role conflict, job insecurity), personal (expectations, personality), physical (illness, poor sleep), daily hassles, frustration and conflict.
Symptoms: physical (headache, fatigue, high BP), emotional (anxiety, irritability), cognitive (poor concentration, worry), behavioural (sleep and appetite changes, withdrawal, substance use).

Measurement: self-report scales — Holmes and Rahe Social Readjustment Rating Scale (life change units), Perceived Stress Scale; physiological measures — heart rate, blood pressure, cortisol, skin conductance; interviews and behavioural observation.
topics.frame: Definition → types or sources as headings with examples → conclusion.

topics.name: Coping with Stress
topics.summary: Definition, nature and goals of coping; coping styles — problem-focused and emotion-focused, approach and avoidance, adaptive and maladaptive.
points: Coping (Lazarus and Folkman): constantly changing thoughts and actions to manage demands that a person sees as taxing or exceeding their resources.
Nature: a process, not a fixed trait; conscious and effortful; changes with the situation.
Goals: reduce harmful conditions, tolerate or adjust to negative events, keep a positive self-image, stay emotionally balanced, maintain relationships.
Problem-focused coping: act on the cause — plan, gather information, solve the problem, seek practical help. Best when the situation can be changed.
Emotion-focused coping: manage the feelings — reappraisal, acceptance, seeking emotional support, relaxation. Best when the situation cannot be changed.
Other styles: approach vs avoidance coping; adaptive (exercise, problem solving, seeking support, humour) vs maladaptive (denial, substance use, withdrawal, aggression).
topics.frame: Definition → styles in a table (style, meaning, example) → conclusion.

topics.name: Effects of Stress: Health, Performance & Relationships
topics.summary: Effects of stress on physical and mental health, on performance and productivity, and on relationships.
points: Health: heart disease and high blood pressure, weaker immunity, headaches, digestive problems, sleep disorders; anxiety, depression and burnout.
Performance (Yerkes–Dodson law): performance rises with arousal up to an optimum, then falls — moderate stress helps, too much hurts.
Productivity: high stress brings errors, accidents, absenteeism, low morale, turnover and poor decisions.
Relationships: irritability, conflict, poor communication, withdrawal, less time and patience for family and friends; stress spreads to others.
Managing the effects: early recognition, healthy lifestyle, coping skills, support at home and work.
topics.frame: Headings (health, performance, relationships) → the inverted-U curve → conclusion.

topics.name: Models of Stress
topics.summary: Fight-or-flight response, General Adaptation Syndrome, the cognitive appraisal model and other models of stress.
points: Fight-or-flight response (Walter Cannon): a threat activates the sympathetic nervous system and adrenaline — faster heart rate and breathing, energy released — preparing the body to fight or flee.
General Adaptation Syndrome (Hans Selye): three stages — alarm (body mobilises), resistance (body adapts, resources used), exhaustion (resources run out, illness follows).

Cognitive appraisal model (Lazarus and Folkman): stress depends on how a person appraises an event — primary appraisal (is it harmful, threatening or a challenge?) and secondary appraisal (can I cope?); reappraisal follows.
GAS vs cognitive appraisal: GAS is physiological and says all stressors produce the same response; the cognitive model is psychological and says the response depends on the person's interpretation.

Life events model (Holmes and Rahe): major life changes add up and raise the risk of illness. Person–environment fit: stress comes from a mismatch between a person's abilities and the demands of the setting.
topics.frame: Name the model and its author → stages or components as a diagram → one example → conclusion.

topics.name: Stress Management Techniques: Relaxation, Meditation, Yoga
topics.summary: Relaxation techniques, meditation, yoga and asanas, mindfulness and biofeedback.
points: Relaxation techniques: deep (diaphragmatic) breathing, progressive muscle relaxation (Jacobson — tense and relax muscle groups), autogenic training, guided imagery.
Meditation: training attention to calm the mind — concentrative (focus on breath, mantra), mindfulness, transcendental. Benefits: lower BP and heart rate, less anxiety, better focus.
Yoga: asanas (postures), pranayama (breath control) and dhyana (meditation) — improves flexibility, calms the nervous system.
Types of asanas: standing (Tadasana), sitting (Padmasana, Vajrasana), lying on the back (Shavasana), lying on the stomach (Bhujangasana), balancing and inverted poses.
Mindfulness: paying attention to the present moment without judging (Kabat-Zinn's mindfulness-based stress reduction).
Biofeedback: electronic monitoring of heart rate, muscle tension or skin temperature so a person learns to control these responses.
topics.frame: Meaning → steps or types → benefits → conclusion.

topics.name: Time Management
topics.summary: Effective and systematic time management, the time management matrix, and techniques of time management.
points: Time management: planning and controlling how time is spent on activities to work effectively and reduce stress.

Time management matrix (Covey, from Eisenhower): Quadrant I — urgent and important (do now); II — important, not urgent (plan; the key quadrant); III — urgent, not important (delegate); IV — neither (eliminate).

Techniques: set SMART goals; prioritise (ABC or matrix); to-do lists; plan and schedule (time blocking); avoid procrastination; delegate; the 80/20 (Pareto) rule; handle interruptions; learn to say no; review daily.
Benefits: less stress, higher productivity, better balance between work and life.
topics.frame: Meaning → matrix as a 2×2 diagram → techniques as headings → conclusion.

topics.name: Cognitive Restructuring (ABCDE) & Problem Solving
topics.summary: Cognitive restructuring and the ABCDE technique of REBT, and problem solving — steps and strategies.
points: Cognitive restructuring: identifying and changing irrational or negative thoughts that cause stress.

ABCDE technique (Albert Ellis, REBT): A — activating event; B — belief about it; C — emotional and behavioural consequence; D — disputing the irrational belief; E — effective new belief and its effect.
Example: failing a test (A) → 'I am a failure' (B) → feeling hopeless and skipping classes (C) → 'one test does not define me; I can prepare better' (D) → feeling motivated and studying (E).
Problem solving steps: define the problem → gather information → generate alternatives → evaluate them → choose the best → implement → review the result.
Strategies: trial and error, algorithms, heuristics (rules of thumb), means–end analysis, working backwards, brainstorming.
topics.frame: Meaning → ABCDE as a table with an example → conclusion.

topics.name: Interpersonal Skills: Communication, Self-awareness, EI
topics.summary: Effective communication, self-awareness, emotional intelligence and conflict resolution as interpersonal skills for managing stress.
points: Effective communication: clear messages, active listening, feedback, appropriate non-verbal signals, empathy and assertiveness — reduces misunderstandings and conflict.
Self-awareness: knowing one's own emotions, strengths, weaknesses and values (Johari window) — the base for managing oneself and relationships.
Emotional intelligence (Goleman; Salovey and Mayer): self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills — helps handle pressure and people.

Conflict resolution: styles — competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding, accommodating (Thomas–Kilmann); steps — understand the issue, listen to both sides, find common ground, agree a solution, follow up.
topics.frame: Meaning → components as headings with examples → conclusion.
